catalog_quote: Words may end either in an underlying vowel or an underlying consonant, and stress generally falls on the penult, although both final stress in disyllables and initial stress in trisyllables was recorded in some forms. new_statements.rule_in_words: In Selau (a Halia dialect) word stress is non-contrastive and by default falls on the penultimate syllable; the author recorded some disyllables with final stress and some trisyllables with initial stress and could not state the conditioning.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress in some disyllables and initial stress in some trisyllables; conditions 'still unstatable'; no minimal pairs for stress could be found. The same page notes that both vowels and consonants occur long ([wakac] 'think' vs [wa:kac] 'lightning').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, based on elicited citation forms (about six hours of elicitation in Canberra in 1975 with two speakers from Torte village, northern tip of Bougainville). Describes the Selau dialect (Glottolog sela1258 under hali1244), not the central Hanahan dialect described by Allen & Allen.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes SELAU (Glottolog sela1258), which Glottolog 5.1 lists as a dialect of Halia (hali1244) and which Allen & Allen 1987 (as reported by Blust) call a 'sub-language' of Halia spoken on the Selau peninsula, N Bougainville; Blust's data are ~6 hours of elicitation in Canberra in 1975 from two speakers from Torte village. The description of Halia proper (central Hanahan dialect, east Buka) is Allen & Allen 1987 Halia Grammar ch. 2 'Sounds', which could not be downloaded by automated download (an automated-access block on sil.org file server) and should supersede/confirm this when read.

new_statements.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress is rarely contrastive and occurs usually on the second or third last syllable. Word final CVC is occasionally stressed too.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (world-2026-09-17, from Blust 2003 on the Selau dialect) codes fixed penult. The OPD agrees that stress is essentially non-contrastive and that the penult is a usual locus, and its 'occasionally' stressed final CVC and antepenult option match Blust's 'final stress in disyllables and initial stress in trisyllables.. movable under still unstatable conditions'. It is weaker than the catalog's classification: it does not privilege the penult over the antepenult, so on this sheet alone the placement is a penult/antepenult window without a stated rule, not fixed penult. Variety differs: the OPD describes Halia of Lemanmanu, Hanakan (Hanahan) and Gogohe on Buka Island; Blust describes Sela…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is (almost) non-contrastive; it usually falls on the penult or the antepenult, with no conditioning stated for the choice; a word-final closed (CVC) syllable is occasionally stressed. No tone or length contrast is described under suprasegmentals (long open vowels are listed as segmental phonemes).
new_statements.exceptions: 'rarely contrastive' (implies a few contrasts, none given); occasional final stress on word-final CVC.
new_statements.identity_note: The catalog record is named Selau (Glottolog sela1258, a mainland north-Bougainville dialect of Halia) and its rule comes from Blust 2003 on Selau. The OPD sheet read here describes Halia [hla] of Buka Passage (villages Lemanmanu, Hanakan/Hanahan, Gogohe), i.e. the Haku/Hanahan dialects on Buka Island, checked by Jan and Jerry Allen, whose fieldwork was on Hanahan Halia.

readall_conflicts: No outright contradiction, but the two statements differ in strength. Blust 2003 (Selau dialect, p.147) says stress 'generally falls on the penult', is non-phonemic, and is 'movable under still unstatable conditions' (final in some disyllables, initial in some trisyllables). The SIL OPD sheet for Halia proper (Buka: Lemanmanu/Hanahan/Gogohe; data checked by the Allens 1994) says stress 'is rarely contrastive and occurs usually on the second or third last syllable' and that word-final CVC 'is occasionally stressed too', i.e. it gives penult and antepenult equal footing and hints at final closed-syllable attraction without stating a weight rule. The catalog's fixed: penultimate syllable coding therefore rests on Blust's 'generally penult'; the OPD supports only 'non-contrastive, right-edge window (penult ~ antepenult, occasionally final CVC)'. The listed work itself (Hemmilä 1998, DP43) could not be opened, so whether its Halia entry (if present) says the same as the 2004 OPD printout is unverified.
